title: Shia theology
hookLine: roots and branches: how Twelver Shia teaching sets out the beliefs that hold everything up

cards: A tree has branches you can see: leaves, fruit, the shade you sit in. And it has roots you can't see, holding the whole thing up. Twelver Shia teaching uses exactly that picture.
Prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, charity: those are furu' al-din, the branches of religion. The beliefs underneath are usul al-din, the roots. And one detail stands out.

In the branches, Twelver Shia Muslims follow a qualified scholar's rulings. In the roots, the teaching goes, each person should hold the beliefs through their own understanding, not just because someone said so.

teach.b: Day 865 gave you the Shia telling of who leads after the Prophet; today, the roots underneath.
Twelver Shia theology names them as tawhid, the oneness of Allah; 'adl, His justice; nubuwwa, prophethood; imama, the imamate; and ma'ad, the return, the resurrection and the Last Day.
Oneness, prophethood and the return appear in Sunni creeds too. Two stand out, and they're today's line. Justice first.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness."

Shia theologians hold that Allah does nothing unjust and nothing without wisdom, and never asks of anyone what they can't do. Here Shia theology stands close to the Mu'tazilah, and the two traditions shared arguments.
Then guidance. Shia teaching holds that Allah does not leave people without a guide.
After the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, guidance continues through imams from his household, beginning with Ali, divinely chosen and protected from error.
In Twelver belief the twelfth imam is alive and hidden, in what's called the occultation, and will return. There's a hadith both Sunnis and Shia know.
In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people: the Book of Allah and the people of his household. Shia scholars read it as pointing to the imams.
Sunni teaching also honors the Prophet's household, but doesn't count the imamate among the roots of faith. Zaydi and Isma'ili Shia have their own accounts too.
Justice and guidance: a God who is fair, and who does not leave people without a guide.

how: Twelver Shia Muslims learn the usul al-din, the roots of religion (tawhid, 'adl, nubuwwa, imama and ma'ad), and are taught to hold them through their own understanding, while following a qualified scholar in matters of practice.

o: the legal rulings a qualified scholar gives on daily practice
the branches of practice: prayer, fasting, pilgrimage and charity
the roots of belief: oneness, justice, prophethood, imamate, return

p: the branches: prayer, fasting and more

s: in Twelver teaching, the roots should be held through your own understanding
following a scholar's rulings is for the branches, like prayer and fasting.
only Shia Muslims know the hadith of the two weighty things
it is in Sahih Muslim; Sunnis and Shia read it differently.
Shia theology stands close to the Mu'tazilah on Allah's justice
both hold that Allah does nothing unjust and asks no one the impossible.

games.q: the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people. what are they, in the hadith in Sahih Muslim?
o: the Book of Allah and the people of his household.
the Kaaba and the city of Medina.
games.why: the Book and his household. Shia scholars read the second as pointing to the imams; Sunnis honor the household without counting the imamate among the roots.

practice: Picture a tree, and let its roots go down one at a time as you name them: tawhid, oneness; 'adl, justice; nubuwwa, prophethood; imama, guidance through the imams; ma'ad, the return.
Go through them again, slower, with just the Arabic words, and stay with the root you'd most like to understand better. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Shia theology. In Twelver teaching, the roots of religion: oneness, justice, prophethood, the imamate, and the return. Today's word.
